title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
claim: Pointwise testing rejects one hypothesis and leaves the question open; scoring a set of competing explanations resolves it to a specific alternative.
layout: 2 stacked panels sharing a central evidence column, left-to-right, bars before/after
description: The figure has two horizontal bands that share one central evidence column. At far left, a dataset icon feeds a robot labeled Hypothesis Generator. Arrows go from it to both bands. The top band, in blue, is titled Contrastive Discovery. It lists three competing explanations H1 to H3 (positive correlation, no correlation, negative correlation), each with a small line icon. Prior belief bars read 0.64, 0.22 and 0.14. The bottom band, in gray, is titled Pointwise. It shows only H1 at 0.64. The alternatives are dashed boxes marked 'Alternatives never stated' with question marks. In the center, an orange Experimental Evidence box has two cycling robot agents and a scatter plot with r≈0. On the right, posterior bars show the contrastive version resolving to H2 at 0.81, with H1 crossed out at 0.07. The pointwise version shows H1 at 0.07 and the other beliefs as question marks, labeled Unresolved in red. The eye goes first to the blue top panel and its check mark.
caption: A contrast set turns a rejection into a resolution. A hypothesis generator proposes a contrast set of three competing explanations (H1–H3) for how X relates to Y, and coder, analyst, reviewer, and reviser agents run an experiment that produces evidence. Bars show elicited belief in each explanation before and after the same evidence. CONTRASTIVE Discovery updates belief over all three explanations and moves the lead from H1 (0.64) to H2 (0.81), so the question resolves to H2 and H1 is ruled out. Pointwise discovery updates belief only in H1 (0.64 to 0.07), so it records a rejection but leaves the question unresolved. See §3 and §4 for details.
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.
